contract: The solver builds an auction module. Sellers list items with an expiration time, and bidders place bids; the module keeps one latest amount per bidder and tracks the highest bid. When a listing expires, driven by time, the seller gets a sale or no-sale notification and each bidder gets a won or lost notification. Listings and bids must be visible within 5 milliseconds.

study.reason: Mapped to handbook case study 8.41. Its title and link are not yet confirmed, so treat the fit as provisional.

depots.name: *bid-depot
depots.partition: hash by the listing's seller id

depots.name: *expire-tick
depots.partition: global tick every 30 s in production; appendable in test mode

pstates.name: $$scheduler
pstates.schema: owned by the TopologyScheduler helper; time-ordered pending listings

topologies.name: auction
topologies.does: stores listings; rejects bids on finished listings, records each bid and raises the top bid, then records the bid for the bidder

topologies.name: expirations
topologies.does: schedules each listing by expiration time and, on each tick, marks due listings finished and writes seller, winner and loser notifications

design.ownership: The seller id owns listings, and every bid on a listing goes to the seller's task, so the finished check, the bidder map and the top bid change on one task. A bid then hops by |hash to the bidder's task. Expiry runs on the seller's task, writes the seller's notification, then reads bidders with a yielding select and hops to each bidder.

stated: Listings are readable and bids visible within 5 milliseconds
Expiry uses simulated time and is driven automatically by time in production
A bidder's earlier bid is replaced only by a higher amount

tested.mechanism: Topology events seen during list-item! and bid! must include a stream topology
The first stream completion around list-item! and around two expiry calls is forced to fail; seller, winner and loser must each get exactly one notification
Some local select during expiry must allow yielding
Each of the three reads must use a RocksDB iterator
20 listings from two clients must have distinct ids

gaps.gap: Retry is not injected on bid!
gaps.wrongDesign: bid! appends the bidder to a per-listing vector and deduplicates on read; a stream retry adds a second entry, and expiry sends that loser two lost notifications

gaps.gap: Read cost of the highest bid is not measured
gaps.wrongDesign: Keep only the bid map and find the maximum on every get-highest-bid; the test listing has 3 bids

gaps.gap: Expiry cost is checked only by the yield flag
gaps.wrongDesign: On each tick, scan every listing on every task with a yielding select and compare expiry times

contract: The solver builds a banking module that tracks each user's balance and the history of transfers in and out. A transfer succeeds only when the sender has enough funds, and failed transfers are still recorded. Every appended deposit and transfer must be processed exactly once, even after failures.

study.title: Payment System
study.reason: The ledger core of the payment system is the nearest match: move money between accounts exactly once and keep a per-account transaction history. The challenge leaves out double entry, idempotency keys and refunds.

pstates.name: $$outgoing-transfers
pstates.schema: {String {String {:to-user-id String :amt Long :success? Boolean}}}, inner map subindexed

pstates.name: $$incoming-transfers
pstates.schema: {String {String {:from-user-id String :amt Long :success? Boolean}}}, inner map subindexed

topologies.name: banking
topologies.does: adds deposits; checks the sender's balance, debits it and records the outgoing transfer, then credits the receiver and records the incoming transfer

design.ownership: The user id owns the balance and both histories. A transfer starts on the sender's task, where the balance check and debit happen together, then makes one |hash hop to the receiver's task for the credit. Reads are direct point and range selects.

stated: Never double process or fail to process an appended deposit or transfer
A transfer id is never appended twice, so no dedupe is needed

tested.mechanism: Every topology event during deposits and 49 transfers must come from a microbatch topology

tested.nfr: Write and read cost per operation
tested.mechanism: A deposit must cost exactly 1 read and 1 write; a transfer at most 8 reads and 6 writes
Reading 50 transfers in or out must cost exactly 1 read, 1 iterator and 50 iterator reads
Deposits to keys generated to hash evenly must give equal depot reads per task, with no partitioner event

gaps.gap: Exactly-once is inferred from topology type; no batch is failed
gaps.wrongDesign: A microbatch forwards the credit through an internal depot to a second microbatch; the type check passes and no test retries a batch
The client checks the sender's balance and appends a transfer already marked as success; two concurrent transfers overdraw the account

gaps.gap: Balance is checked for deposits only
gaps.wrongDesign: Transfers go through |global to one task; the partitioner check wraps only the deposits

contract: The solver builds the backend of a Slack-like chat product: registration with unique handles, profiles, presence, rooms with membership, messages and threads. It also keeps per-user unread counts, a mentions inbox and a recent-threads feed. The protocol sets 5 ms visibility for writes, fixed-work paginated reads and a workload of 2,000 messages and 100,000 heartbeats per second.

study.reason: Mapped to handbook case study 8.55. Its title and link are not yet confirmed, so treat the fit as provisional.

pstates.name: $$thread-replies
pstates.key: root message id, then reply id

pstates.name: $$room-seq
pstates.key: room id; count of room messages ever

pstates.name: $$room-reply-counts
pstates.key: room id, then root message id

pstates.name: $$mentions
pstates.schema: {Long {UUID {:room-id Long :sender Long :content String}}}, inner map subindexed
pstates.key: mentioned user id, then message id

pstates.name: $$rt-by-act
pstates.key: user id, then latest activity id

pstates.name: $$rt-idx
pstates.key: user id, then root message id

topologies.name: core
topologies.does: claims handles and room names, writes profiles and stores accepted messages and replies

topologies.name: derived
topologies.does: maintains membership, read cursors, unread sequences, reply counts, mentions and recent threads

topologies.name: heartbeat
topologies.does: records a heartbeat in in-memory presence on the user's task

topologies.name: presence
topologies.does: reports whether a user's last heartbeat is recent

topologies.name: online-filter
topologies.does: keeps the online users from a chunk of member ids

topologies.name: room-page
topologies.does: reads 20 room messages with reply counts and current names

topologies.name: thread-page
topologies.does: reads 20 thread replies with current names

topologies.name: recent-threads
topologies.does: reads 20 recent threads by activity with their metadata

topologies.name: unread-counts
topologies.does: subtracts each room cursor from the room sequence for every room the user is in

topologies.name: mentions-page
topologies.does: reads 20 mentions with the sender's current name

design.ownership: Handles and room names are claimed on their own hashed task, so exactly one concurrent claim wins. All other writes arrive on the acting user's task, then hop to the room, root message or mentioned user that owns each view. Presence is an in-memory task global on the user's task and writes nothing durable.

stated: Workload: 10M users, rooms up to 50,000 members, 2,000 messages and 100,000 heartbeats per second
Registration, profiles, room creation and posts visible within 5 ms
Exactly one winner among concurrent claims of a handle or room name
Fixed read work for paginated reads; unread counts cost O(1) per room; reads take about 50 ms
Online means a heartbeat within the last 120 seconds; presence need not be fully reliable
Only the 200 most recently active threads are visible

tested.mechanism: 100 heartbeats write fewer than 10 records; a post to a 300-member room writes fewer than 40; mark-room-read! writes fewer than 15 and reads fewer than 60
Absolute read bounds on room page, unread counts, recent threads, mentions and online members over deep history
Reads right after register!, create-room! and post-message!, with no processing barrier
8 concurrent registrations and 8 concurrent room creations for one name have one winner; 30 concurrent posts each land and count once
Every durable view is exact after update-module! and presence resets; 205 threads leave exactly the 200 most recent

gaps.gap: No retry injection for derived counters
gaps.wrongDesign: A stream topology increments a per-room message counter for unread counts; a stream retry counts the message twice

gaps.gap: Visibility is checked on return, not by time or topology type
gaps.wrongDesign: post-message! appends to a microbatch and blocks until the batch commits; reads without a barrier pass

gaps.gap: The 120-second presence window is not tested, and the reference uses 30 seconds
gaps.wrongDesign: Any presence window passes; a user who heartbeat 60 seconds ago shows offline in the reference

contract: The solver builds a module that stores profiles and posts and delivers each post to the timeline of every follower, reading a bundled social graph module with very unbalanced follower counts. Fanout must not write durably per follower, so timelines live in memory and must be rebuilt after a restart. Fanout must be balanced across tasks and fair between large and small accounts, and timeline reads do fixed work over the 800 newest entries.

study.title: Social Media Feed
study.reason: The feed case study's fanout-on-write problem maps directly: deliver each post to follower timelines, keep celebrity fanout from stalling other posts, and bound what a timeline stores. Case study 8.45 is the follow-on; its title and link are not yet confirmed.

depots.name: *process-tick
depots.partition: global tick every 1 s in production; appendable in test mode

pstates.name: $$pending-fanouts
pstates.key: [poster id, post id, social graph task] to the last follower delivered

pstates.name: $$mirror-followers
pstates.key: target account id, on each task that holds a slice

topologies.name: writes
topologies.does: stores profiles and each post in the poster's log

topologies.name: fanout
topologies.does: reads up to 1,000 followers per task per batch, saves a cursor for the rest, and appends deliveries to in-memory timelines once per batch

topologies.name: get-user-timeline
topologies.does: returns an account's own posts in order

topologies.name: compute-timeline-init
topologies.does: collects recent posts from followees to rebuild a timeline

topologies.name: reconstruct-timeline
topologies.does: fills a user's in-memory timeline after a restart

topologies.name: get-timeline
topologies.does: reads 20 entries from the in-memory timeline and adds current names and content

design.ownership: The poster owns profile and post log. Fanout reads each follower slice on the social graph task that holds it and delivers by follower id to an in-memory timeline on the follower's task. Timeline reads hop by |hash to the reader, then to each poster for name and content.

stated: No PState or depot write per follower during fanout; in-memory state must be recoverable
Fanout is balanced across tasks
Fanout is fair: one post's delay on another does not grow with follower count
No permanent backlog; a user posts at most once every 5 seconds
Profiles and own timeline visible within 5 ms; timeline reads do fixed work; 800 entries visible

tested.mechanism: A post to 500 followers writes fewer than 20 RocksDB records, and all 500 followers see it
After update-module!, a reader's timeline of 30 posts is rebuilt exactly and in strict order, and new fanout still works
After 850 posts, paging returns exactly the newest 800

gaps.gap: Balance is untested; the test's 500 followers sit on one social graph task
gaps.wrongDesign: Gather all followers with the get-followers query and deliver from the poster's task

gaps.gap: Fairness is untested, and the reference's chunking path never runs
gaps.wrongDesign: Deliver a post's whole follower list in one event, or chunk and drop the remainder

gaps.gap: Recovery depth is sized to the reference's limit of 10 posts per followee
gaps.wrongDesign: Rebuild only the last 10 posts of each followee; the test posts exactly 10 per followee, and the reference does the same

contract: The solver builds one module that keeps each account's followers and followees and delivers posts to follower timelines. Disk work must be near-optimal and CPU even across tasks for any follower distribution, from mostly tiny accounts to many accounts with 10,000 to 100,000 followers. The fanout constraints match the fanout challenge: no durable write per follower, balanced and fair fanout, and recovery after restart.

study.title: Social Media Feed
study.reason: The feed case study covers both halves: storing a skewed follow graph and fanning posts out to timelines without letting celebrity accounts overload one server.

depots.name: *process-tick
depots.partition: global tick every 1 s in production; appendable in test mode

pstates.name: $$partitioned-followers-control
pstates.key: target account id; lists the tasks that hold its followers

pstates.name: $$partitioned-follower-tasks
pstates.key: target account id, then follower id to task

pstates.name: $$partitioned-followers
pstates.key: target account id, on each task that holds a slice

pstates.name: $$pending-fanouts
pstates.key: [poster id, post id, follower task] to the last follower delivered

topologies.name: social-graph
topologies.does: updates followees and places each follower on a task for the target, adding a task every 1,000 followers

topologies.name: writes
topologies.does: stores profiles and each post in the poster's log

topologies.name: fanout
topologies.does: reads up to 1,000 followers per task per batch, saves a cursor for the rest, and appends deliveries to in-memory timelines once per batch

topologies.name: get-followers
topologies.does: reads the target's task list and gathers each follower slice with yielding reads

topologies.name: get-user-timeline
topologies.does: returns an account's own posts in order

topologies.name: compute-timeline-init
topologies.does: collects recent posts from followees to rebuild a timeline

topologies.name: reconstruct-timeline
topologies.does: fills a user's in-memory timeline after a restart

topologies.name: get-timeline
topologies.does: reads 20 entries from the in-memory timeline and adds current names and content

design.ownership: The follower owns its followee set. The target's home task owns the task list and follower-to-task index; a target keeps followers on one task until 1,000, then spreads new ones to other tasks by direct routing. Fanout reads each slice on the task that holds it and delivers by follower id to in-memory timelines.

stated: Even CPU across tasks and near-optimal total disk work for every follower distribution
Load: at most 5,000 followees, about 7,000 posts and 100 follows per second
No PState or depot write per follower during fanout; balanced, fair fanout with no backlog
Follow and unfollow are idempotent
Profiles and own timeline visible within 5 ms; timeline reads do fixed work; 800 entries visible

tested.mechanism: A post to 500 followers writes fewer than 20 RocksDB records, and all 500 followers see it
After update-module!, a reader's timeline of 30 posts is rebuilt exactly and in strict order, and new fanout still works
Both directions, idempotent follow and unfollow on graphs of at most 5 followers; the suite assumes no partitioning strategy

gaps.gap: Balance and near-optimal work are untested
gaps.wrongDesign: A plain follower set hashed by target puts a celebrity's followers and fanout on one task
Scatter every account's followers across all tasks; balanced, but each small-account post touches every task

gaps.gap: Follow and get-followers costs are not measured
gaps.wrongDesign: A non-subindexed follower set is read and rewritten whole on each follow
